result: Tetrahymena thermophila has seven mating types that recognize non-self partners through direct cell-cell contact, leading to costimulation characterized by tip transformation and Con-A receptor appearance, followed by stable pairing between heterotypic cells.
evaluation: Claims C1-C9 establish the basic biology of T. thermophila mating-type recognition. These claims are well-supported by citations to established literature (Nanney, 1953; Cervantes et al., 2013; Orias et al., 2017) and visual evidence from figures and videos. The claims describe well-characterized phenomena in this model organism.

result: Mating type is determined by two head-to-head genes MTA and MTB, each encoding transmembrane proteins with mating-type-specific extracellular regions. Both genes are non-redundant and essential for mating, as deletion of either gene severely impairs or abolishes mating.
evaluation: Claims C10-C15 describe the genetic basis of mating-type determination, supported by prior work (Cervantes et al., 2013) and structural analysis. The conclusion that both genes are essential and non-redundant is based on deletion phenotypes showing ΔMTB cells cannot mate and ΔMTA cells mate very poorly.

result: Neither ΔMTA nor ΔMTB cells can fully transmit or receive mating signals to/from wild-type cells, and both MTA and MTB proteins must be present in the same cell to transmit the mating-type signal, ruling out a simple receptor-ligand model.
evaluation: Claims C18-C25 present key experimental findings from pre-incubation experiments (Figure 2B). The data clearly show that deletion mutants cannot costimulate WT cells, and mixing ΔMTA and ΔMTB cells together does not rescue the phenotype. This strongly supports the conclusion that both proteins must be in the same cell and argues against a simple receptor-ligand model.

result: Costimulation involves two separable stages: Con-A receptor appearance (requiring only MTB in partner cells) and tip transformation (requiring both MTA and MTB). Neither ΔMTA nor ΔMTB cells can fully stimulate or be stimulated by WT cells.
evaluation: Claims C28-C38 describe detailed phenotypic analysis of costimulation markers (Figures 2C, 2D). The data show differential requirements for MTA and MTB in the two hallmarks of costimulation. The observation that ΔMTA cells can induce Con-A receptors but not tip transformation is well-documented and supports the two-stage model.

result: MTA and MTB cannot functionally complement each other when expressed on different cells, but ΔCDK19 and ΔCYC9 cells (expressing both MTA and MTB) can stimulate WT cells, leading to the hypothesis that MTA and MTB form a mating-type recognition complex (MTRC).
evaluation: Claims C39-C42 integrate experimental observations to propose the MTRC hypothesis. The contrast between ΔMTA+ΔMTB mixing (no complementation) and ΔCDK19/ΔCYC9 pre-incubation (successful stimulation) provides strong logical support for the hypothesis that MTA and MTB must physically interact in the same cell.

result: IP-MS experiments show that MTA and MTB co-purify with each other and with six additional proteins (MRC1-MRC6), suggesting they form a mating-type recognition complex (MTRC).
evaluation: Claims C43-C48 describe IP-MS results (Figure 3B, 3C). The co-purification of MTB with MTA, and the identification of MRC1-6 proteins that interact with both, provides strong biochemical evidence for a protein complex. The use of multiple baits (MTA, MTB, MRC1) and appropriate controls strengthens the findings.

result: All MTRC components are large membrane proteins (92-212 kDa) with diverse predicted functions including GFR domains, pectin lyase-fold, Ca2+ translocators, and nucleotide hydrolases. Most MRC genes are highly coexpressed with MTA and MTB, but only MTA and MTB sequences are mating-type-specific.
evaluation: Claims C49-C56 characterize the MTRC components through bioinformatic analysis and genome sequencing (Figure 3D, 3E). The domain predictions and coexpression data are well-documented. The finding that only MTA/MTB are mating-type-specific is confirmed by whole genome sequencing of multiple mating types.

result: CDK19, CYC9, CIP1, and AKM3 were identified in IP-MS with few peptides but are coexpressed with MTA/MTB and essential for mating, suggesting they interact with MTRC and may be involved in downstream signaling.
evaluation: Claims C57-C62 identify additional proteins that may interact with MTRC. While the IP-MS evidence is weaker (few peptides), the coexpression data (Figure 3E), prior work on CDK19/CYC9/CIP1 (Ma et al., 2020), and the new finding that ΔAKM3 cannot pair provide converging support for their involvement in mating-type signaling.

result: MTA7-HA is a membrane protein exposed on the cell surface but does not localize to cilia, as demonstrated by cell fractionation, biotinylation, and mass spectrometry.
evaluation: Claims C63-C66 establish the subcellular localization of MTA through multiple complementary approaches (Figure 4A-D). Cell fractionation shows membrane association, biotinylation confirms surface exposure, and both IP-WB and MS consistently show absence from cilia. The convergence of multiple methods provides strong support.

result: MTB2-eGFP overexpression produces a functional protein that localizes to the cell surface (not cilia) in a linear pattern along ciliary rows. The strain exhibits selfing ability and mates with all types except VI and II, supporting the self-recognition model.
evaluation: Claims C67-C76 use fluorescent tagging to visualize mating-type protein localization (Figures 4F, 4G). The functional validation (normal mating with most types), microscopy showing surface localization adjacent to cilia, and MS confirmation of absence from cilia provide strong support. The selfing phenotype provides additional insight into the recognition mechanism.

result: The mating-type-specific extracellular regions of MTA and MTB mediate non-self recognition. Treatment with MTAxc or MTBxc from different mating types significantly increases pairing rates in a dose-dependent manner, with synergistic effects when both are present.
evaluation: Claims C77-C85 present stimulation experiments using recombinant extracellular domains (Figures 5A-C, 6A-H). The data show consistent, statistically significant increases in pairing rates across multiple mating-type combinations and concentrations. The synergistic effect of combined treatment supports the interaction between MTA and MTB. The dose-response curves strengthen the findings.

result: The mating-type-specific regions of MTA and MTB also mediate self-recognition. Treatment with cognate MTAxc/MTBxc decreases initial pairing rates with synergistic effects, though this inhibition is eventually overcome by 4 hours.
evaluation: Claims C86-C92 demonstrate self-recognition through inhibition experiments (Figures 5D-F, 6I-J). The data show statistically significant decreases in early pairing rates when cells are treated with cognate mating-type proteins, with synergistic effects. The time-course showing eventual recovery is well-documented. Together with non-self recognition data, this supports the dual recognition model.

result: MTA and MTB form a multifunctional protein complex that mediates both self- and non-self mating-type recognition, representing a dual approach to mating-type recognition in T. thermophila.
evaluation: Claims C93-C98 present the main conclusions of the study, integrating findings from deletion mutants, IP-MS, localization, and stimulation experiments. The evidence from multiple experimental approaches converges to support the model that MTA/MTB form a complex that can distinguish self from non-self. This represents a novel mechanism in mating-type recognition.

result: Unlike basidiomycetes and flowering plants that use either self- or non-self recognition, T. thermophila uses both. The significant variation in mating-type region length among Tetrahymena species suggests different species may use different recognition mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C99-C101 place the findings in evolutionary context. The comparison to other systems is supported by citations, and the observation about length variation among Tetrahymena species is from prior work (Yan et al., 2021). The speculation about different mechanisms is reasonable given the data, though it remains to be tested.

result: MTRC is likely over a million Daltons. Self-recognition may generate inhibitory signals or inactivate MTRC, possibly through Ca2+ changes mediated by MRC4/MRC5. Non-self recognition activates MTRC, potentially involving CDK19 complex and AKM3.
evaluation: Claims C102-C107 present speculative mechanistic models. While the size estimate is reasonable based on component sizes, the signaling mechanisms are largely speculative. The Ca2+ hypothesis is based on analogy to other systems and predicted function of MRC4/MRC5, but lacks direct experimental evidence. The involvement of CDK19 and AKM3 is inferred from weak interactions and phenotypes but not demonstrated.

result: The MTB2-eGFP strain can self and mate with all types except VI and II. This supports the self-recognition model and suggests that self-recognition generates no or weak inhibitory signals, as the strain contains both homotypic (A6B6) and heterotypic (A6B2) MTRCs.
evaluation: Claims C108-C112 analyze the selfing phenotype of the MTB2-eGFP strain. The mating pattern (selfing, mating with most but not all types) is experimentally demonstrated. The interpretation involving two types of MTRCs is logical given the genetic composition. The conclusion about weak inhibitory signals is a reasonable inference from the selfing ability.

result: Paramecium tetraurelia has two mating types determined by expression or non-expression of a Tetrahymena-MTA/B-like protein called mtA.
evaluation: Claim C113 provides comparative context from a related ciliate. This is supported by citations (Singh et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2021) and represents established knowledge about Paramecium mating systems.

result: Most species have two sexes/mating types and use either self- or non-self recognition, but some lineages (ciliates, basidiomycetes) have multiple mating types, and some plants have multiple-allele self-incompatibility systems.
evaluation: Claims C114-C117 provide general background on sexual systems across biology. These are well-established facts supported by appropriate citations (Goodenough and Heitman, 2014; Heitman, 2015; Phadke and Zufall, 2009; Iwano and Takayama, 2012).

result: CDK19, CYC9, and CIP1 are coexpressed with MTA and MTB, are essential for mating, and form a cyclin-dependent kinase complex that localizes to the cell tip and pairing junction.
evaluation: Claims C16-C17 summarize prior work by the authors (Ma et al., 2020). These findings are cited and provide important context for understanding the current results, particularly the weak IP-MS interactions with these proteins.

result: T. thermophila has two nuclei (MAC and MIC). The MIC mat locus contains multiple mating-type gene pairs in tandem, while the MAC has only one pair. During conjugation, mating-type gene pair loss and intranuclear coordination occur, with mating type becoming fixed after ~60 fissions.
evaluation: Claims C118-C123 describe the nuclear biology and mating-type determination process in T. thermophila. These are well-established features of Tetrahymena biology supported by citations (Zhou et al., 2022; Orias et al., 2017) and provide essential background for understanding the experimental system.
